b: The most anticipated game of all time is here with the drop of “Grand Theft Auto VI,” over a decade after the last title in this landmark franchise. Knowing that a generation of expectation meant that they couldn’t just run it back again, the developers at Rockstar cut no corners in producing this instant classic. It’s a masterpiece of immersive storytelling that perfectly blends deep player customization with some of the richest screenwriting, world creation, and voice work in the history of gaming.

It’s hard to know where to begin unpacking what works about “GTAVI” because one key to this game’s success is the variance in its gameplay. One minute, you’re blasting your way through a drug den in what looks like the Florida Keys; the next you’re doing home repairs or hanging on the couch with your buddy Cal, playing in-game video games.

The story starts with a meet-cute over a stolen car between joint protagonists Jason and Lucia, two of the most complex and unforgettable characters of their gaming generation. Early on, Lucia goes to jail, so you play as Jason for a few hours as you adjust to the game world, but you will eventually do joint and solo missions, swapping between the two loyal partners. They are three-dimensional, rich avatars, roles that adjust to basics of customization like outfits and styles, but people who also feel grounded by writers. You can make Jason & Lucia your own, but every version of them feels true to the story that this game wants to tell at the same time.

What is that story? Where does one even begin with a five-chapter narrative that unfolds over dozens of missions and at least 50 hours of gameplay—most people who take the time with every subplot and secret this world contains will be here for well over 100, maybe even 200, by the way. This is a game you let unfold in front of you instead of feeling pulled along on a rail. Jason & Lucia go from petty crimes in this world’s version of the Florida Keys to wealthy crime lords in the towers of Vice City, modeled so closely after Miami that I laughed when I realized how closely a hotel I stayed at four years ago in the Sunshine State’s city had been replicated.

Without spoiling, Jason & Lucia climb the ladder of the criminal underworld in the Southeast corner of the United States to make enough money to get out from under the thumb of the crime bosses who control them. From cocaine drops off the southern coast to bank heists in the city, they push through with the goal of keeping their lives together at all costs. It’s a game about systems that attempt to destroy you and how you have to stay united to fight back against them.

It leads to dozens of missions involving rich supporting characters, all set in a world that has something new to show you around every corner. And it’s all conveyed with sharp, timely writing that even has a thing or two to say about pop culture in the 2020s, especially in arcs involving a pair of rappers known as Dimez and the way you use social media via an in-game phone that’s basically your HUD. You can call cabs, text characters, and even just surf when you’re bored at night. Yeah, you can get distracted by your smartphone in a game, too.

It’s clichéd to say that an open world game has everything, but “GTAVI” has everything. It attains a density of gameplay that approaches “The Sims and the Furious” in its level of real-world detail that makes you literally take detailed care of your protagonists, including not just hundreds of possible outfits, haircuts, and tattoos, but regular stops to eat and even work out. Don’t worry: While I found the diversions enjoyable, very little of this is necessary.

Much has been made of the reveal that cars actually run out of gas in this universe, but if that’s the kind of menial task you don’t want in your GTA, all you have to do is steal another one. Workouts, meditation spots, and other minor tasks can improve your character’s condition, but you can also power through with brute force, even if the game will warn you that you’re hungry and tired.

What’s perhaps most impactful to the storytelling, in terms of customizable detail, is the need to put work into your relationship. Whether it’s choosing to do missions together, checking in via text, or even just holding hands, the state of your relationship impacts how things unfold. It becomes one of the most memorable relationships in the history of gaming, never leaving the center of the quiet or loud moments of the experience.

And that blend of quiet and loud is never less than enthralling. Some missions here effectively blow out the speakers like the climax of a Hollywood blockbuster, but others are quirky and memorable in a very different way. The writers keep dipping into wonderful cinematic influences including “The Fast and the Furious” movies, “Heat,” “Die Hard,” “Miami Vice,” and the work of Michael Bay. But they also take time for a very Rockstar kind of wonder, often in the breathtakingly rendered universe of Leonida. There’s never been a game with more detail, from the way rush hour impacts traffic to the dozens of forms of wildlife dotting the landscape.

The impression that this world is alive in a way a gaming world never has before comes from the hundreds of NPCs who honestly feel like they’re living their own independent lives. Everyone you pass has their own identity, and they’ll interact with you differently based on your aggression or response. If you sideswipe someone on the road, don’t be surprised if he runs you off it out of road rage.

One day early on, I stumbled onto someone’s property by accident; he pulled out a gun, I took him down, and opened his garage to grab a few things for my trouble. None of this is required. It’s one of hundreds of examples of locations and people that you might never meet but that make this world so unforgettable. I did an entire mission involving a chimp sanctuary just this week that I’m pretty sure was entirely optional, but I just happened to encounter it.

The developers of “GTAVI” value things that matter to film and video game fans, including production design, cinematography, and even soundtrack. Dozens of artists have contributed new tracks, including Travis Scott, Dua Lipa, Future, and many more, and cars have radio stations with over a dozen channels that rarely repeat. The use of music in the game is more effective than in most blockbusters, with the writers dropping in new and familiar tunes to enhance missions, while also employing a consistently great score.

As for other tech aspects, it’s not just a one-to-one Miami riff but a shifting world of incredibly varied locations, from the meth dens of the Everglades to the high-rises of the big city. The sound design also deserves praise, as music blasts out of passing cars or conversations can be overheard at cafes. There’s arguably never been a gaming world this rich with vibrant life, and the slightly controversial fact that it’s 30FPS never diminished my experience on a PS5 Pro. When Rockstar says it was the only way to make this detailed, dense world feasible on a console, you’ll know what they mean after mere minutes of playing.

Of course, you can traverse it in various ways. There are hundreds of cars—one could spend so much time just finding the right ones to sell to dealers or customize for their own use—but there are also chapters involving air and water travel. Flying over Leonida on drug drops amplifies the beauty of this setting even further, while escaping on a jet ski gives it even more “Miami Vice” adrenaline.

“Grand Theft Auto VI” has already become a $1-billion-plus success, a game that’s dominating pop culture before it’s even released. And yet fans should know they’ve only seen the beginning of what this game has to show them. It’s more of a world to explore than a game to play, and it’s a world that you’ll never forget. [100/100]
The Publisher provided a review copy of this game on PS5. It is also available on Xbox on November 19.
